title: Kid Rena and the New Orleans rhythm sections
summary: Rena made high notes before Louis; Nicholas says the old rhythm sections had a natural beat.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Could we talk a little bit about the rhythm sections in those days? Yeah. You said that the Bunk band in 44 was a hark back to the old style prior to 1920 because Bunk hadn't played for those years. Yeah. Would you say that the rhythm section, that was Baby Dodds, Slow Dragon, Lawrence Marrero, Elton Purnell, all came later. Would you say that that rhythm section was similar to the ones before 1920?

I will say it, yes. You know, they had the original beat. I'll be truthful with you. I didn't hear any bad rhythm sections from New Orleans. Even now, I don't think they have this thing, it's a natural. They get to our bass and drums and things, they play together. They play for the other guys. They didn't do a lot of solo work, but they played together. It was a beautiful thing. They didn't blast or nothing in those days, you know. It was full. We didn't need a piano. No.
It's the timing. It's the- They had rhythm.

They were born with it. It seemed like- Well, that's another thing. I don't remember having to practice no rhythm. I was practicing notes because it was a natural thing. We walked in rhythm and little kids, five or six years old, hum a tune, they hear a tune, played by a band on the corner, and the next day they're all whistling. It was a natural thing. I didn't know you had to study rhythm and all that stuff until later on through the years. We have to, you don't.
